opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the directions I'm most excited about.

In the original framework, the agents are basically norm-compliant by assumption. They're trying to figure out what the shared rules are by watching others, and once they've inferred a norm, they follow it, either because they intrinsically value compliance or because that's just part of their utility function. That works if you're modeling well-meaning newcomers to a community. But it obviously leaves out a big part of the story, which is that many people follow norms partly because they expect consequences if they don't.

So the extension is to let agents reason not just about "what is the norm?" but also "what happens to me if I violate it?" An agent with selfish preferences, one that would happily free-ride, can still end up behaving cooperatively if it models other agents as likely to sanction violations. You get a kind of nested inference. I'm inferring the norm, and I'm also inferring how others will react to deviations from it, and that changes what's actually in my interest.

What's nice about doing this in a Bayesian, model-based way is that the sanctions don't have to be observed directly. You can anticipate them. If I see that people in a community tend to punish certain behaviors, or even that they disapprove of them, I can generalize. I don't have to get punished myself to learn that free-riding is a bad bet. That matters, because in the real world a lot of norm enforcement is latent. It's the threat of sanction, not the frequency of it, that holds things together.

It also helps explain how norms stay stable. If there's a population of agents that enforce norms, even a minority, and free-riders anticipate that enforcement, you can get compliance that's far more robust than if everyone just had to happen to share the same values. And you can start asking more interesting questions: when do sanctions have to be credible? What happens when enforcers are uncertain about whether a violation actually happened? How do second-order norms, norms about punishing violators, emerge?

From an AI alignment perspective, I think this is important because we don't want to assume every agent we build, or every agent our systems interact with, is perfectly cooperative. We want systems that understand the social structure they're embedded in, including the incentives that sustain cooperation. I'd still prefer to build agents that actually value the norms, not just ones that comply out of fear of punishment. But modeling sanctions is part of understanding why human normative systems work at all, and it gives us a richer account of how norms get learned, enforced, and maintained over time.

r001.rationale: It says a selfish agent inclined to free-ride may cooperate because it anticipates other agents will sanction violations, making compliance serve its interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot, because the honest answer is that the framework as it currently stands mostly assumes the agents are cooperative. In the norm-learning work, the agents are trying to infer the norms of a group from observing behavior, and then they comply with those norms more or less because they've internalized them. That's a reasonable model of a lot of human behavior, actually, but it obviously leaves out the case you're pointing at, which is the agent that learns the norm perfectly well and then decides it would rather not follow it when nobody's watching.

So the way I'd think about extending it is roughly in two layers. The first layer is that sanctions themselves are norms. If I'm an agent coming into a group, I'm not just learning "people share food" or "people queue at the counter," I'm also learning "when someone cuts the line, other people glare at them, or refuse to deal with them later, or in some cases actively punish them." That second-order structure is observable in the same data, and in principle the same Bayesian inference machinery can pick it up. You see a violation, you see what happens after the violation, and you update on both what the rule is and what the enforcement regime looks like. There's a nice connection here to the Ostrom tradition in institutional economics, where graduated sanctions are one of the design principles for sustaining common-pool resource management, and to some of the evolutionary work on third-party punishment.

The second layer is the decision-theoretic one. Once an agent has a model of the enforcement regime, a self-interested agent can do planning under that model. It can ask, if I free-ride here, what's the probability I get caught, what's the expected cost, how does that trade off against the benefit. And the nice thing is that this gives you a very clean account of why norms are stable even in populations that contain some free-riders. If enforcement is credible enough, the anticipated sanction makes compliance the rational choice even for an agent that doesn't care about the norm intrinsically. You get compliance without internalization.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I actually think a purely sanction-based account is incomplete, and maybe even a bit dangerous as a design philosophy for AI systems. If the only reason an agent complies is anticipated punishment, then the moment it believes it can evade detection, or the moment it becomes powerful enough that sanctions can't be enforced against it, the compliance disappears. That's precisely the failure mode people worry about with advanced AI. So I'd want sanctions to be one component of a richer picture, where some agents, and ideally the AI systems we build, do in fact come to value the norms themselves, or at least value the cooperative arrangement the norms sustain, rather than treating them as external constraints to be optimized around.

There's also a really interesting computational question, which is how an agent decides whether to participate in enforcement. Punishment is costly. If I sanction you, I'm paying some price, and the benefit accrues to the whole group. So enforcement is itself a public good, and you get a second-order free-rider problem. The resolution in the human case seems to involve things like reputation, metanorms, which is the norm that you should punish people who don't punish, and probably some amount of genuine emotional investment, like people really do feel indignation. Modeling that computationally is hard, but I think it's exactly the kind of thing where the norm-learning framework could be extended, because metanorms are again just more structure in the observable data.

So to summarize, I'd say anticipated sanctions are a very natural extension, they fall out of treating enforcement as part of what's being learned rather than something bolted on, and they explain how you get stability with heterogeneous motivations. But I'd resist the move of making them the whole story, both because empirically humans don't seem to work that way, and because normatively, for AI, we want agents whose good behavior is robust to the absence of a watcher.

r001.rationale: The response says a self-interested agent weighs the probability and cost of being caught, and that credible anticipated sanctions can make compliance rational even without intrinsic concern for the norm.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish learning a norm from being motivated to follow it. An agent might understand perfectly well that it’s supposed to contribute to a public good, but still prefer to free-ride if contributing is costly and it can benefit from everyone else’s contributions.

Anticipated sanctions could enter the planning process as a consequence of violating the norm. The agent would reason about whether someone will observe the violation, whether they’re likely to respond, and what that response might cost. That could be a direct punishment, but it could also be losing access to future cooperation. If the expected cost is sufficiently high, compliance becomes worthwhile even for an agent that doesn’t intrinsically care about the norm.

The interesting complication is that sanctions have to be credible. If punishing is costly, why would another agent do it? So this extension would also need to account for the motivations of the people enforcing the norm. Otherwise, we’ve just moved the free-rider problem one level up.

And we’d want to preserve the distinction between someone complying because they endorse a norm and someone complying because they expect sanctions. They can look identical while being observed, but behave very differently when they think they can get away with a violation.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent inclined to free-ride may comply when it expects others to observe and sanction a violation, because the expected cost can make compliance worthwhile even without intrinsic concern for the norm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key extension is to distinguish learning what the norm is from being motivated to follow it. An agent could infer perfectly well that it’s supposed to contribute to a public good and still decide that it would rather free-ride.

Anticipated sanctions give that agent an additional reason to comply. It has to predict whether others will detect a violation, whether they’ll respond, and how costly that response will be. That could be an explicit punishment, but it could also be reputational damage or exclusion from future cooperation. Those expected consequences then enter its planning alongside the benefit of free-riding.

The interesting part is that those expectations depend on learning about other agents: not just what norms they recognize, but which ones they’re willing to enforce. And then you have the further question of why anyone would bear the cost of enforcement. So sanctions could extend the framework to more self-interested agents, but explaining how that enforcement becomes credible is an additional piece of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent inclined to free-ride may comply because it anticipates detection and costly consequences from others, weighing those expected costs against the benefit of free-riding.
